content:
It's questionable whether working on things that contribute to development of AGI will have net positive impact on the world - and the risk is big that it will not. At the same time, I don't feel it should be a factor to not work on formal verification. One way out is to accept that one's work contribute towards AGI and take part in this race, in the role that is clear to not support the "yolo-style" agi developments. I'm not yet sure where is the boundary, but there definitely is a boundary between working on (say) GPT6 and between working on (say) aesop2 - both of which contributing towards automated reasoning.

Where are your boundaries of the automated reasoning direction you want to contribute towards, and the direction you would prefer to not see and experience? How to take out that negative factor from our work when planning a career around Lean which, without doubt, will at least be tightly coupled to autoformalization developments? I'm curious what's your opinion as the general lean community
#Machine Learning for Theorem Proving or #Autoformalization

I'm inclined to suggest this is getting off-topic for this forum. (Particularly in #general, but maybe even in the AI and Lean channels.) A "how do you feel about X" question invites low quality noise from anyone. Anyone responding, please try to prove me wrong by making sure your responses are concise, insightful, or ideally point to existing discussions elsewhere. (Or, better, have this discussion on the discord instead.)

Discussions on discord are easily lost in a flood of messages. Those who have specific opinions should post here so that their replies can be preserved and easily found later. Discord is not the ideal place for collecting well thought out opinions on a topic that affects the whole community.

Yes, I wouldn't say that my question is strictly about ai4math or autoformalization - more on the side of how much should recent technological advancements affect the direction of early career in 2026?.

And I agree it can attract low-quality opinions, but the crux questions are quite difficult and I wouldn't like the discussion to get lost: given a formalization project, how to tell:

  1. Will it be beneficial for the Lean community?
    There is a very good ongoing discussion about it in other thread - a shiny formalization project might not be long-term beneficial for the community. A particular example are projects that lead to finishing some theorem in an ugly way that will never make it to Mathlib, leading to no incentive to continue the work from people that do the same but taking care to keep their code high-quality. An interesting opinion is that of:
    Patrick Massot said:

I think the situation is pretty clear: AI companies, and especially MathInc, will indeed thoroughly bomb this area to turn it in a giant radioactive wasteland that will never be able to sustain life again, so we will never get the benefits expected from formalization (improved understanding and accessibility). I strongly advise young people to contribute to less shiny projects that are less likely to be destroyed.

  1. Will it be useful for the general society? Will you get funding for it?
    An interesting datapoint here are the slides of yesterday's presentation at AITPM by Kevin Buzzad - perhaps getting the FLT project to the original formulation from 1980's is of very high interest to companies.
    Companies surely get funding and surely the general society is impressed by compute "replacing" human expert work in some fields. However, it doesn't necessarily make a sense to take on such a project as individual when there probably is a whole team doing the same.

Here I'm interested - what do you think are, right now, the most important projects:

  • that lead to long-term improvement in our communal formal verification capabilities. So: easier manual proof-writing in Lean
  • that are at least big enough for a phd-style project
  • that, if finished, would lead to an incentive deep in the future - just long enough for companies to not want to work on that
    One good thing is working on automated theorem proving tactics: improving grind, try? or whatever. But are these the most important directions we currently have?
  1. If I get scooped, is there any reward from finishing my work?
    For some projects, the incentive from the community is rather independent from the rent-paying, grant-receiving incentive. In what ways are PhD students incentivized to work on projects that are important, but might not necessarily make a publication?

Even if some company sniped FLT formalization overnight, all the tiny bits of work going to that project also contribute towards having more very high-quality code in Mathlib. So the incentive from the community is still there and not that affected, it will not pay your rent however.
I want to highlight a blogpost by @Seewoo Lee on this topic: https://seewoo5.github.io/jekyll/update/2026/03/05/early-mathematician-ai.html
